newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries gain on strong note auction.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries gain on strong note auction.

text.p: Strong demand at a five-year note Treasury auction lifted the entire U.S. credit market on Thursday, analysts said,

Treasury sold $12.5 billion in five-year notes at an awarded yield of 6.409 percent. The bid-to-cover ratio -- the gauge of bidding interest -- came out at 2.57-to-1, the highest level since May, and above the average of the past 12 five-year note sales.
"It looked like a pretty strong auction, reasonably well bid," said chief economist Paul Kasriel at Northern Trust.
Kasriel said the economic releases of the day set a positive tone for the market at the opening and fueled buying later in the session.
Also, jobless claims rose 11,000 in the last reporting week to 340,000 -- a sign that some market analysts viewed as a hint of slower job market.

"All economic data today were supportive of a stronger market," Kasriel said. "The only quirk was that unfilled orders for aircraft fell and that does not square with what we know about the industry. Boeing new orders are continuing to fly in and the company is hiring."

Amid a generally positive tone, the front end continued to benefit from the Federal Reserve's decision on Tuesday to leave short-term interest rates unchanged. The decision triggered a relief trade since the market had priced in a 25-basis-point rise in the 5.25-percent federal funds rate.

"The numbers are soft and the Fed did not do anything. A lot of people who have been holding off to see what the Fed was going to do want to get something on the books as we're coming up on quarter-end," Kasriel added.
Three- and six-month bill rates closed down five and two basis points, respectively, to 4.88 percent and 5.05 percent.
The front end had already drawn strength on Wednesday from a well-bid Treasury two-year note auction.

"Tomorrow, the only thing that is important is the final reading on the University of Michigan (for September,)" said senior economist Astrid Adolfson at MCM MoneyWatch of the closely watched gauge of consumer sentiment.
Adolfson did not expect major buying interest on Friday as some key players remain cautiously sidelined.
"I expect to mostly see the speculative players, the trading accounts, the day traders tomorrow because there is nothing of importance in terms of data," Adolfson said.

Adolfson added major investors are also following the dollar's performance -- it has regained momentum versus both the mark and the yen lately -- and other major sovereign debt markets before making a decision.
Year-bill rates fell three basis points to 5.34 percent.

Prices of the two-year notes rose 3/32 to 99-29/32, yielding 6.05 percent. Five-year notes rose 4/32 at 100-11/32, yielding 6.42 percent and the 10-year note climbed 8/32 to 102-14/32 to yield 6.66 percent.
